title: Stalker (1979 film)
description: 1979 Soviet epic science fantasy film by Andrei Tarkovsky
wiki_lead:
Stalker (Russian: Сталкер, IPA: [ˈstaɫkʲɪr]) is a 1979 Soviet post-apocalyptic drama film directed by Andrei Tarkovsky with a screenplay written by Arkady and Boris Strugatsky, loosely based on their 1972 novel Roadside Picnic. The film tells the story of an expedition led by a figure known as the "Stalker" (Alexander Kaidanovsky), who guides his two clients—a melancholic writer (Anatoly Solonitsyn) and a professor (Nikolai Grinko)—through a hazardous wasteland to a mysterious restricted site known simply as the "Zone", where supposedly exists a room which grants a person's innermost desires. The film combines elements of science fiction and fantasy with dramatic, philosophical, and psychological themes.
The film was shot over a year on film stock that was later discovered to be unusable and had to be almost entirely reshot with a new cinematographer, Alexander Knyazhinsky. Stalker was released by Goskino in May 1979. Upon release, the film garnered praise in the Soviet and Warsaw Pact press, but only mixed reviews in the West. In later years it was recognised as one of the greatest films of all time. In the decennial critics' and directors' polls published by the British Film Institute's magazine Sight and Sound in 2022, Stalker placed 43rd and 14th, respectively. The film sold over 4 million tickets, mostly in the Soviet Union, against a budget of 1 million roubles.

Plot
"The Zone" is a huge tract of open land where the normal laws of physics supposedly do not apply, containing supernatural hazards. At the heart of the Zone lies a "Room" that is said to grant the wishes of anyone who steps inside. The government has fenced off the Zone, subjecting "Stalkers", people who illegally guide others through the Zone, to harsh prison time if caught crossing the border.
One Stalker has just returned from a long prison sentence to his wife and daughter. To his wife's horror, a disaffected writer and a physics professor immediately hire the Stalker to take them through the Zone. Needing the money, he meets the Writer and Professor in a rundown bar-café, warning them that they must do what he says to survive the dangers that lie ahead. He explains that the Zone is a living thing that visitors must respect.
The trio evades the Zone's military guards by following a train through the gate, riding through the Zone's vast wilderness on a railway work car. The Zone contains such human remnants as old abandoned industrial facilities, corpses, guns, and tanks. The Stalker cautiously tests for anomalies as they painstakingly make their way toward the Room, though nothing unusual occurs.
The three men discuss their reasons for wanting to visit the Room as they travel: the Writer fears losing his inspiration, the calm Professor hopes to analyze the Zone in order to win a Nobel Prize, and the Stalker insists he has no motive beyond the altruistic aim of aiding the desperate to their desires. grok_lead: Stalker is a 1979 Soviet science fiction art film written and directed by Andrei Tarkovsky. The narrative centers on an anonymous guide known as the Stalker who escorts a Writer and a Professor through a desolate, hazardous region called the Zone, evading military patrols to reach a enigmatic Room purported to grant one's deepest wishes. Loosely adapted from the 1972 novel Roadside Picnic by brothers Arkady and Boris Strugatsky, the film diverges significantly from the source material, emphasizing metaphysical and existential themes over pulp science fiction elements. Filmed primarily in abandoned industrial sites near Tallinn, Estonia, including a disused power plant contaminated with chemical pollutants, production spanned five years amid numerous setbacks, such as script revisions demanded by Soviet authorities and multiple restarts due to technical failures. Tarkovsky's distinctive styleâcharacterized by extended long takes, deliberate pacing, and natural soundscapesâserves to immerse viewers in contemplative ambiguity, probing questions of faith, authenticity, and human motivation without resolving them narratively. Upon release, Stalker garnered critical acclaim for its philosophical depth and visual poetry, achieving a perfect 100% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes based on contemporary reviews, though its slow tempo polarized audiences accustomed to faster-paced cinema. The film's enduring influence spans cinema, literature, and video games, inspiring works that explore anomalous zones and inner quests, while posthumous accounts link the harsh shooting conditions to health deteriorations for Tarkovsky and lead actor Anatoly Solonitsyn, both of whom succumbed to lung cancer shortly after.
